strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: extending linear probes to polynomials that can be evaluated progressively (truncated) or cascaded, giving a 'safety dial' and an adaptive, input-conditional compute mode for safety monitoring. This fills a genuine gap between static cheap probes and expensive always-on LLM monitors.

The methodology is technically sound and clearly presented: progressive (degree-wise) training to guarantee good truncated submodels, symmetric CP factorization to control parameter growth and enable faithful pairwise attribution, and a simple cascade algorithm. The insight that truncation requires special training (vs. training the full polynomial) is demonstrated convincingly in Fig. 4 and ablations G.1.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: 4 LLMs (up to 30B, including a reasoning model), 2 large-scale safety datasets (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails), multiple layers, 5 seeds, parameter-matched baselines (linear, bilinear, separate MLPs, early-exit MLP) with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps, plus extensive ablations (rank, max degree, symmetric vs. non-symmetric CP, calibration, per-subcategory results, latency/throughput).

The cascaded evaluation result (near-full-polynomial performance at compute only slightly above the linear probe) is practically significant, and the built-in feature attribution (Sec. 4.4) is a genuine advantage over MLP probes, honestly framed with its limitations.
The paper is well-written, limitations are candidly discussed, and code is promised to be available.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and primarily compositional: TPCs build on existing polynomial networks (Dubey et al., 2022; Chrysos et al.), progressive training on greedy layer-wise training (Belilovsky et al., 2019), and cascading on early-exit networks (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Romdhani et al., 2001). The application domain and the truncation-aware training are new, but each ingredient is established.

Absolute performance gains are often modest: F1 improvements over strong baselines (EE-MLP) are frequently within or near the seed-variance bands in Fig. 2, and the headline 'up to 10% over linear probes / 6% over EE-MLP' applies only to specific harm subcategories and models. Some test plots (e.g., gpt-oss, Llama) show EE-MLP competitive or better in places.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: binary sequence-level harmfulness on two public datasets only. There is no evaluation on output/response monitoring, jailbreak/attack settings (e.g., many-shot jailbreaking), distribution shift, or adversarial cases, which limits claims about real-world safety utility. Mean pooling over tokens is also a strong simplification that is not ablated against alternative pooling.

The 'compute' metric is parameter count, which is only a proxy; the latency study helps but shows EE-MLPs are faster at small batch sizes, and the claimed practical advantage depends on the serving regime.

The feature attribution is dense and difficult for humans to interpret (acknowledged by the authors), so the interpretability claim is weaker in practice than the framing suggests; higher-order interactions beyond pairwise are not really interpretable.
Small-data behavior and regularization needs are acknowledged as unexplored, leaving an open question about robustness of the method outside the large-scale regime studied.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea—truncated evaluation of a progressively trained polynomial as a dynamic safety monitor—is easy to follow and reasonably motivated.

Experimental breadth is decent: 4 LLMs (up to 30B), 2 large safety datasets, multiple layers, parameter-matched baselines (linear, bilinear, MLP probes, early-exit MLP), 5 seeds, and extensive ablations (rank, max degree, symmetric vs non-symmetric CP, latency/throughput, calibration).

The progressive training scheme is a sensible contribution over prior polynomial networks (Dubey et al., 2022; Chrysos et al., 2022), and Fig. 4 plus appendix ablations (G.1) convincingly show that truncated submodels only perform well when trained progressively.
Per-subcategory analysis (Fig. 9) and the cascade analysis (Fig. 3) add useful granularity beyond aggregate F1, and computational cost analysis (Appendix E, G.2) is a nice touch.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is essentially a combination of existing components—polynomial networks with symmetric CP factorization (Dubey et al., 2022), greedy layer-wise training (Belilovsky et al., 2019), and early-exit cascades (BranchyNet, Romdhani et al., 2001)—applied to the linear-probe setting. The 'test-time compute for safety' framing overstates what is a fairly incremental architectural tweak.

Headline gains are weak and inconsistent: on the main WildGuard benchmark the F1 differences over EE-MLPs are often within noise or only a few tenths of a point (e.g., gemma-3-27b L40 test: ~88.5 vs ~88.2), and on several models the TPC does not clearly beat simpler baselines. The striking 'up to 10%/6%' improvements only appear for narrow subcategories selected post hoc, which risks cherry-picking.

Missing evaluations critical to the claimed application: safety monitors must be robust to adversarial/jailbreak inputs and distribution shift, yet there are no adaptive-attack or OOD experiments (e.g., evaluating probes trained on WildGuard against jailbreak sets like HarmBench or AdvBench). Given the safety motivation, this omission is serious.

The val/test gap (e.g., ~98 vs ~88 F1 on gemma-3) suggests substantial distribution shift, and the paper does not analyze generalization across datasets or probes trained on one model and transferred to another, which limits the practical significance of the 'safety dial' story.

Two evaluation modes are largely trivial: fixed-truncation scaling is just evaluating a smaller model, and the cascade is a standard confidence-threshold early-exit. The headline claim that the cascade yields full-model accuracy at near-linear-probe cost is expected behavior for any nested-classifier cascade, not a specific contribution of TPCs.

Interpretability claims are overstated: Section 4.4/limitations admit the learned interactions are dense and 'lack obvious legibility to humans'; neuron indices (e.g., neuron 4830) are uninterpreted, so the 'built-in feature attribution' provides little actionable insight beyond what gradient attribution on an MLP could give.

Using parameter count as the primary compute metric is a weak proxy; while latency experiments exist, they are only for one model and show TPCs are slower than EE-MLPs at small batch sizes (the regime most relevant for always-on monitoring).

Hyperparameters (N=5, R=64, layer choice) appear tuned on validation sets of the same datasets the test sets are drawn from, and there is no small-data-regime or regularization study (acknowledged in limitations), which weakens claims of generality.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and cleanly executed: truncated polynomial classifiers extend linear probes with higher-order interactions that can be trained progressively and evaluated at any truncation level, giving a genuine 'compute dial' and a natural cascade mechanism that is new for activation-based safety monitoring.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: 2 large-scale safety datasets (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails), 4 LLMs up to 30B parameters, multiple layers, 5 random seeds per configuration, and parameter-matched baselines (linear, bilinear, separate MLPs, EE-MLP) each with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps.

A rich set of ablations supports design choices: progressive vs. standard training (Figs. 4, 10-11), CP rank (Figs. 13, 15, 17-19), maximum degree (Fig. 14), symmetric vs. non-symmetric CP (Fig. 16), and calibration (Fig. 8).

The cascading defense analysis (Fig. 3) is convincing: near-full-model F1 at a fraction of the net compute, and the latency/throughput benchmark (Fig. 12) addresses the concern that parameter count is only a proxy for real cost.
The symmetric CP factorization enables faithful neuron-pair attribution (Eq. 6, Fig. 5), giving a concrete, mechanistically grounded interpretability story that MLP baselines cannot match.
Honest limitations section, available code, clear notation and writing throughout.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each ingredient exists separately—polynomial probes (White et al. 2021), CP-factorized polynomials (Dubey et al. 2022), greedy layer-wise training (Belilovsky et al. 2019), early-exit cascades (BranchyNet), polynomial kernels for probing. The contribution is a well-engineered combination applied to safety probing rather than a fundamentally new method.

Aggregate improvements over strong baselines are modest: F1 differences over EE-MLP are often within a few tenths of a point and partly within seed variance (e.g., BeaverTails results across all models), and on some model/layer combinations TPCs underperform baselines. The headline 10%/6% claims are per-subcategory maxima (best-case figures), which overstates typical gains.

The evaluation is limited to binary prompt-level classification with mean pooling; no response-level monitoring, no distribution-shift or adaptive-attack robustness testing, and no comparison to LLM-based monitor baselines (e.g., Llama Guard) despite motivating the paper against them.

For a safety application, the metrics focus on F1; there is no analysis of false-negative rate at low false-positive operating points, which matters most for guardrails, and no discussion of the failure mode of the cascade exiting early on a confidently wrong linear probe.

Hyperparameter choices (N=5, R=64) are validated, but the method's benefit is dataset-specific (much larger gains on WildGuardMix than BeaverTails), so the generality of the claimed accuracy-scaling behavior remains partially unverified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: extending linear probes to higher-order polynomials whose terms can be evaluated progressively, providing an 'anytime' safety monitor with a compute-accuracy dial and an input-conditional cascade. This is a natural and useful extension of existing probe-based safety monitoring.

Extensive and well-organized empirical evaluation: 4 LLMs (up to 30B params), 2 large-scale safety datasets (WildGuardMix, BeaverTails), multiple layers, 5 random seeds, parameter-matched MLP/EE-MLP/bilinear baselines with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps.

Thorough ablation studies in the appendix: rank sweeps, maximum degree, symmetric vs non-symmetric CP, progressive vs standard training, latency/throughput benchmarks, calibration (ECE), per-subcategory breakdowns, cross-dataset generalization (HarmBench, ToxicChat, OpenAI-moderation), and comparisons against LLM-as-monitor guard models.

The progressive training scheme is validated: Fig. 4 and Appendix G.1 clearly show standard joint training fails to produce well-performing truncations, supporting the paper's central claim over prior polynomial networks.

Built-in pairwise neuron attribution (Eq. 6, Fig. 5) is a genuinely useful property of the symmetric CP form, distinguishing TPCs from black-box MLP probes; honest limitations section acknowledges the dense/low-legibility nature of the attributions.
Good reproducibility: codebase, hyperparameter sweeps, PyTorch pseudocode, detailed computational cost analysis (FLOPs), and latency/throughput benchmarks at realistic batch sizes.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the components are individually well-known (polynomial probes by White et al. 2021, CP-factorized polynomial networks by Dubey et al. 2022, early-exit cascades by BranchyNet/cascaded classifiers). The contribution is primarily their combination (truncated/progressive evaluation of polynomials as cascades) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Headline performance gains are modest and sometimes within noise: on BeaverTails, TPCs are behind EE-MLPs on test F1 for 3/4 models; on WildGuardMix, differences over MLP/EE-MLP at full depth are small (~0.2-0.5 F1). The main gains over linear probes apply only to specific subcategories, and the paper itself notes performance is often non-monotonic in compute, undermining the clean 'scaling' narrative.

Interpretability claims are oversold relative to the evidence: the pairwise attribution analysis is a single qualitative example; the authors concede in the limitations that the interactions are dense and lack obvious human legibility, so the practical interpretability benefit remains largely unproven.

Compute is measured primarily by parameter count, which is a coarse proxy; although latency benchmarks are provided, they are limited to one model/layer, and the latency advantage holds only at medium/large batch sizes.

The cascading defense is a fairly straightforward application of early-exit ideas to the polynomial structure; no comparison against learned/optimized routing policies or confidence calibration tuned for the cascade.

The comparison to LLM-as-monitors is confounded: external LLMs were not fine-tuned on WildGuardMix and used a single non-optimized system prompt, so the claimed superiority of activation probes over 8B-class monitors should be interpreted cautiously.

Scope is narrow: binary sequence-level harmfulness classification with mean-pooled activations at a single (manually selected) layer; no jailbreak/adversarial robustness evaluation, no output-side monitoring, and no exploration of the small-data regime.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: making activation-based safety monitors adaptive to compute budgets, which is a sensible direction given that most requests are benign.

The experimental setup is broad: 4 LLMs (up to 30B params), 2 large-scale safety datasets, multiple layers, and 5 random seeds per run, with extensive appendix ablations (rank, maximum degree, symmetric vs. non-symmetric CP, latency/throughput, calibration, cross-dataset transfer).

The progressive training scheme (Sec. 3.2.1) is a reasonable and clearly motivated contribution, and Fig. 4 convincingly shows that standard polynomial training does not yield well-performing truncations while progressive training does.

The cascade evaluation (Alg. 1) with confidence-threshold early exit is well-executed, and the parameter-matched comparisons against EE-MLPs and MLP baselines, with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps, are fair.
Code release, PyTorch pseudocode, hyperparameter details, and FLOP analysis support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core model is a symmetric CP-factorized polynomial classifier (Dubey et al., 2022; Chrysos et al.) applied as a probe (cf. White et al., 2021's polynomial probe), and the cascade mode is a straightforward application of early-exit ideas (BranchyNet; Viola-Jones). The contribution is largely a recombination of known components rather than a fundamentally new method.

The headline gains are small and fragile. On the primary benchmark (WildGuardMix test), TPC (88.50) improves over MLP probes (88.20) by only 0.3 F1; on BeaverTails test, TPC is behind EE-MLP for 3 of 4 models (Table 1b). 'Competes with or outperforms' is the actual result, not a clear win, and no statistical significance tests are reported despite 5 seeds.

A large and unexplained gap between validation and test F1 (~98 val vs ~87-89 test on WildGuard) is visible throughout the paper and never analyzed. This raises serious questions about what the probes are learning and whether the reported 'safety dial' improvements reflect robust generalization or dataset-specific artifacts.

The central 'safety dial' narrative is undermined by the authors' own admission that TPCs and MLPs 'often fail to yield monotonically increasing performance with additional test-time compute' (Figures 2, 8, 11, 12). A developer who 'buys' more guardrails cannot reliably know they get stronger safety, which weakens the practical value proposition.

The interpretability claims are overstated. The attribution analysis (Sec. 4.4) is a single anecdotal prompt, and the authors concede the neuron-combination attributions are 'dense and lack obvious legibility to humans.' 'More interpretable than MLPs' is asserted but never evaluated with any user study or quantitative interpretability metric.

Compute is measured by parameter count, which the authors acknowledge is only a proxy; the latency study shows EE-MLPs are faster at small batch sizes, which is precisely the regime relevant to per-request always-on monitoring.

Scope is narrow: only binary harmful/harmless classification with mean-pooled single-vector representations. No evaluation on adversarial/jailbreak-specific probes, no comparison to the strongest LLM-as-judge fine-tuned monitors, and the LLM-as-monitor comparison in Appendix F.3 is admittedly preliminary with un-optimized prompts.

The cross-dataset results (Table 3) show low precision across all models, further supporting that these probes learn dataset-specific labeling conventions rather than a general safety concept, which the paper acknowledges but does not resolve.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing LLM safety monitors are static in compute cost, and the paper argues convincingly for dynamic, input-conditional monitoring, connecting to the test-time compute paradigm.

Simple, elegant, and technically sound core idea: a degree-N polynomial trained progressively term-by-term yields N nested sub-classifiers, enabling both a 'safety dial' (fixed-order truncation) and an adaptive cascade with early exit; the additive form guarantees the linear probe is recovered exactly at n=1.

Extensive and careful evaluation: 4 LLMs (up to 30B params), 2 large-scale safety datasets, 16 layers, 5 random seeds, parameter-matched baselines (linear, bilinear, MLP, EE-MLP) each with dedicated hyperparameter sweeps, plus many ablations (rank, max degree, symmetric vs non-symmetric CP, progressive vs joint training).

Cascade evaluation is well-analyzed across confidence thresholds, showing near-full-model accuracy at a fraction of net compute; honest reporting that EE-MLPs are faster at small batch sizes while TPCs are competitive/faster at realistic batch sizes.

Valuable additional analyses: cross-dataset generalization (HarmBench, ToxicChat, OpenAI-moderation), comparisons to LLM-as-monitors and guard models, calibration analysis, per-harm-subcategory breakdown, and mechanistically grounded pairwise neuron attribution made possible by the symmetric CP factorization.
Good reproducibility: code release, detailed hyperparameter sweeps, PyTorch pseudocode, FLOP/latency cost analysis, ethics and LLM-usage disclosures, and a candid limitations section.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the model form (CP-factorized polynomials) follows Dubey et al. (2022), cascading follows early-exit literature (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016), and parameter-matched EE-MLPs already provide a similar dynamic-defense capability; the main new elements are progressive/truncated training and the application to safety monitoring.

Absolute performance gains are modest and often within seed-level noise: on BeaverTails, TPC test F1 trails EE-MLPs for 3/4 models, and improvements over MLP/EE-MLP baselines on WildGuardMix are small (fractions of an F1 point), even though the cascade-efficiency story is stronger.

Compute is proxied by parameter count; while empirically validated against FLOPs/latency, the latency results reveal EE-MLPs are faster at small batch sizes, tempering the cost claims in the always-on single-request regime that the paper emphasizes.

Feature attribution, though mechanistically faithful, is dense and lacks human legibility (acknowledged by the authors); it is demonstrated on only a single prompt and model, so the interpretability contribution remains preliminary.

Scope is limited to binary sequence-level harmful/harmless classification on mean-pooled activations; no evaluation on jailbreak-style adaptive attacks, output monitoring, or streaming settings where dynamic monitors are arguably most needed.

Optimal layer choice must be searched per model, and performance is not monotonically increasing with test-time degree for any model form; the paper lacks a principled solution, deferring both to future work.
